description: A minimal two-species predator-prey model. The prey population X grows exponentially in the absence of predators at rate alpha and is removed by predator-prey encounters at rate beta (mass-action / random-encounter term beta*X*Y). The predator population Y decays exponentially in the absence of prey at rate gamma and grows by converting consumed prey into new predators at rate delta (term delta*X*Y). The model exhibits the classic neutral centre of closed orbits with a conserved quantity, producing sustained oscillations whose amplitude depends on initial conditions.

variables.name: X
variables.description: Prey population density (e.g. number of prey, in arbitrary/relative units)

variables.name: Y
variables.description: Predator population density (e.g. number of predators, in arbitrary/relative units)

parameters.name: alpha
parameters.description: Intrinsic per-capita growth rate of the prey in the absence of predators

parameters.name: beta
parameters.description: Predation (attack) rate coefficient for prey removal via predator-prey encounters

parameters.name: delta
parameters.description: Predator reproduction efficiency: conversion of consumed prey into new predators

parameters.name: gamma
parameters.description: Per-capita death rate of the predator in the absence of prey

origin.source_text: self-derived (no source literature; standard Lotka-Volterra formulation)
assumptions: Closed, well-mixed (homogeneous) population with no spatial structure or age structure.
Prey have unlimited food and grow exponentially (Malthusian) when predators are absent; no prey carrying capacity.
Predation is modelled as a mass-action (random-encounter / bilinear) term proportional to the product X*Y.
Predators have no alternative food source and die at a constant per-capita rate gamma.
A fixed fraction of consumed prey biomass is converted into new predators (constant conversion efficiency delta); no predator saturation (type I functional response).
All rates (alpha, beta, delta, gamma) are constant in time and independent of population density.
Populations are large enough that demographic stochasticity is negligible (deterministic ODE).
Parameters are chosen to be biologically reasonable: predator conversion efficiency delta < prey removal coefficient beta, and the two populations oscillate on comparable timescales.

missing_information: No empirical data are provided because this is a self-derived model; alpha, beta, delta, gamma are illustrative values, not fitted to a specific system.
The units of population density (individuals vs. biomass) are arbitrary/relative.
No carrying capacity, predator satiation, or time delays are included; these would be needed to match real ecological time series more closely.
